audience.programmeDescription: Law at Tilburg University studies legal rules, institutions and reasoning in their social context. The Dutch-taught LLB develops private, criminal, constitutional, administrative, European and international law, practical skills and legal research, with an approved minor and a required thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial legal study with politics, society, economics, ethics and empirical methods. Its options prioritise law in social context, sustainability and governance, or legal practice and organisations. Tilburg provides a more extensive Dutch doctrinal and procedural sequence; the course relationships shown are partial.

componentNotes.y1-intro-law: The general Law LLB is taught in Dutch, with individual English-language courses. The non-credit Dutch language test and student-development activities are retained outside the 180-EC total.
componentNotes.y1-administrative: This introduction builds on first-year constitutional law. The course is completed after the autumn constitutional introduction.
componentNotes.y2-property: Second-year property, contract, liability and criminal courses deepen the respective first-year foundations. Completing all first-year courses supplies those foundations.
componentNotes.y2-criminal-procedure: The dedicated procedure course builds on Introduction to Criminal and Criminal Procedure Law and Procedural-Law Practical Skills from Year 1.
componentNotes.y3-philosophy: The dated Legal Philosophy B course examines the EU as a legal and political union, including representation, legitimacy, direct effect and supremacy.
componentNotes.y3-moot-court: Entry requires at least 90 EC at registration; credits obtained after registration do not satisfy that threshold. The course includes mandatory attendance, legal-source research, written procedural documents, pleading training and an oral moot court. This pathway completes both earlier years before registration.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The 8-EC thesis begins in the autumn and spans the academic year. At least 90 EC must be earned when teaching begins. For students who started in September 2025 or later, a completed Tilburg Skills Lab is also required. Both earlier years and the non-credit Skills Lab are completed before Year 3. The thesis develops an independent legal research question, framework, proposal and paper; no particular legal topic is assumed.
componentNotes.y3-minor: Eighteen EC remain for an approved minor: Law in Practice, Law and a Sustainable Future, an outside minor or an approved custom package. No particular minor is imposed. The optional exchange requires separate approval and substitution under the regulations; it is not added to this 180-EC minor pathway.

cellNotes.text: The general Law LLB is taught in Dutch, with individual English-language courses. The non-credit Dutch language test and student-development activities are retained outside the 180-EC total.
This introduction builds on first-year constitutional law. The course is completed after the autumn constitutional introduction.
Second-year property, contract, liability and criminal courses deepen the respective first-year foundations. Completing all first-year courses supplies those foundations.
The dedicated procedure course builds on Introduction to Criminal and Criminal Procedure Law and Procedural-Law Practical Skills from Year 1.
The dated Legal Philosophy B course examines the EU as a legal and political union, including representation, legitimacy, direct effect and supremacy.

Entry requires at least 90 EC at registration; credits obtained after registration do not satisfy that threshold. The course includes mandatory attendance, legal-source research, written procedural documents, pleading training and an oral moot court. This pathway completes both earlier years before registration.

The 8-EC thesis begins in the autumn and spans the academic year. At least 90 EC must be earned when teaching begins. For students who started in September 2025 or later, a completed Tilburg Skills Lab is also required. Both earlier years and the non-credit Skills Lab are completed before Year 3. The thesis develops an independent legal research question, framework, proposal and paper; no particular legal topic is assumed.

Eighteen EC remain for an approved minor: Law in Practice, Law and a Sustainable Future, an outside minor or an approved custom package. No particular minor is imposed. The optional exchange requires separate approval and substitution under the regulations; it is not added to this 180-EC minor pathway.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.text: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
